title: Intarsia crochet
subtitle: Working blocks of colour without carrying yarn across the back of the work
excerpt: Intarsia crochet uses separate yarn supplies for each distinct colour area in a design, rather than carrying all colours across every row. When a colour block ends, the yarn is left hanging and the next colour is picked up directly. This keeps the fabric single-layer and avoids the thick floats that tapestry crochet produces. Intarsia is suited to large, sharp-edged geometric colour blocks.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing). Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: A single contiguous area of colour in an intarsia design. Each block uses its own separate yarn supply and the yarn is not carried across to neighbouring blocks.
A small spool or card used to hold a small quantity of yarn for intarsia work. Using bobbins rather than full balls prevents the separate yarns from tangling together as the work progresses.

content.text: use a separate yarn supply for each distinct colour section. When the first colour block ends, that yarn hangs at the back and the next colour is picked up from its own ball or bobbin. The yarns are not carried across the row: they wait at the point where each colour block begins. This contrasts with tapestry crochet, where all colours are carried and crocheted over continuously. Intarsia suits large, well-defined colour areas where the float of carrying yarn across would be long enough to distort the fabric.

items.name: Yarn bobbins or small cards
items.note: Wind each colour separately to prevent tangling. One bobbin per colour per block.

items.name: Tapestry needle
items.note: For weaving in the many ends that intarsia produces.

content.text: Wind each colour into separate bobbins. One colour block = one bobbin. If a colour appears in two separate blocks on the same row, use two bobbins of that colour.

Work across the row in the first colour until reaching the colour change point. On the last yarn-over of the last stitch before the colour change, draw through the new colour to complete the stitch. The old colour hangs at the back.
Work across the second colour block with the new
. Do not carry the previous colour across; leave it hanging where it was dropped.

When the next colour change is reached, pick up the next bobbin and change colour in the same way. At any point where two yarns meet, twist them around each other once before continuing to prevent a gap forming at the join.
At the end of each row, disentangle the bobbins before turning. Keep the bobbins from different blocks separated so they do not twist around each other as the work turns.

items.symptom: Gaps are forming at the colour join lines
items.cause: The two yarns at the junction point were not twisted around each other before continuing.
items.fix: At every junction between two colour blocks, bring both yarns up together and cross them once before continuing. This locks the join and closes the gap.

items.symptom: The bobbins are tangling badly on every row
items.cause: Multiple bobbins are hanging freely and twisting together as the work turns.
items.fix: Only unwind enough yarn from each bobbin for one or two rows at a time. After each turn, deliberately untwist the bobbins before starting the next row.

items.symptom: The colour join line shows a diagonal step instead of a straight vertical line
items.cause: The colour change was made one stitch too late or too early on alternating rows.
items.fix: Count stitches to the colour change point on every row. The join should happen on the same stitch position every row to produce a straight vertical edge.

content.text: Work a simple 3-colour stripe block: 20 stitches wide, divided into 3 columns of roughly equal width in different colours. Work 10 rows. This practice piece produces all the colour join and bobbin-management situations that appear in larger intarsia projects, at a manageable scale.
